title: CUET Geography Test 2
subject: Geography / Geology (Code: 313)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Geography - 313.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) domain-paper format and public Geography shift analyses (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Fundamentals of Human Geography (rationalised)
NCERT Class 12 India: People and Economy (rationalised)
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage or table; the set stays together.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: International Trade
questions.question: Which port of India is a landlocked harbour, connected to the sea by a channel cut through solid rock and sand, and is described by NCERT as the deepest landlocked and well-protected port?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Visakhapatnam
Why: NCERT describes Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh in these terms; it was developed to handle iron ore, petroleum and general cargo.
Why not the others: Kolkata (A) is a riverine port on the Hugli; Paradip (C) is in the Mahanadi delta; Chennai (D) is one of the oldest artificial harbours on the east coast.
Key point: Bhilai and Bailadila supply iron ore for export through Visakhapatnam.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Water Resources
questions.question: Over-use of groundwater has led to an increase in the concentration of arsenic in the groundwater of parts of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) West Bengal and Bihar
Why: NCERT notes that excessive withdrawal of groundwater has raised fluoride levels in parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra and arsenic levels in parts of West Bengal and Bihar.
Why not the others: Rajasthan and Maharashtra (B) are linked with fluoride, not arsenic; NCERT does not name (C) or (D) for this problem.
Key point: Falling water tables and poorer water quality are both results of over-withdrawal.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Population
questions.question: A state has a population of 6.2 crore and an area of 1,55,000 square kilometres. What is its density of population?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 400 persons per sq km
Given: population = 6,20,00,000; area = 1,55,000 sq km.
Step 1: Density = population ÷ area.
Step 2: 6,20,00,000 ÷ 1,55,000 = 400 persons per sq km.
Common mistake: losing a zero while dividing (4,000, option B); dividing area by population gives a tiny figure that is not a density.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Planning and Sustainable Development
questions.question: The Hill Area Development Programme, launched in the Fifth Five Year Plan, initially covered 15 districts. These included:
options: A) All districts of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir
B) The desert districts of western Rajasthan and Kachchh
C) The coastal districts of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
D) Hill districts of Uttarakhand, Darjeeling and the Nilgiris
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Hill districts of Uttarakhand, Darjeeling and the Nilgiris
Why: NCERT says the HADP covered all the hilly districts of present Uttarakhand, the Mikir Hills and North Cachar Hills of Assam, Darjeeling in West Bengal and the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the districts named in NCERT.
Key point: Hill areas with more than 600 m height and not covered under the Tribal Sub-Plan were treated as backward hill areas.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Mineral and Energy Resources
questions.question: Jharia, the largest coalfield of India, is followed in size by Raniganj. Both lie in which river valley?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Damodar
Why: NCERT notes that most Gondwana coal is in the Damodar valley (Jharkhand–West Bengal coal belt); Jharia is the largest coalfield, followed by Raniganj.
Why not the others: The Godavari (A), Mahanadi (B) and Son (C) valleys also have coalfields, but not Jharia or Raniganj.
Key point: Tertiary coal occurs in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Transport and Communication
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about satellite communication and cyberspace:
(A) Satellites have made the cost and time of communication almost the same whatever the distance.
(B) Cyberspace exists only in places that are connected by fixed telephone lines.
(C) India has made great strides in satellite development and uses it for communication and broadcasting.
(D) The internet has widened services such as e-commerce, e-learning and e-governance.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A) NCERT notes that with satellites, communicating over 500 km costs the same as over 5,000 km. (C) and (D) also follow NCERT.
Why not the others: (B) is false — cyberspace is the world of electronic computerised spaces encompassed by the internet, reached through satellites and wireless links too. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Cyberspace is everywhere — in offices, on ships and planes, wherever there is a connection.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.question: Noise pollution — the unbearable, uncomfortable sound from sources such as factories, construction, vehicles and aircraft — is measured in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Decibels
Why: NCERT notes that the level of steady noise is measured by its sound level in decibels (dB).
Why not the others: Hertz (A) measures frequency, pascals (B) measure pressure and joules (D) measure energy.
Key point: Noise pollution is location-specific: its intensity falls with distance from the source.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Human Settlements
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Town)
(A) Pataliputra
(B) Lucknow
(C) Kolkata
(D) Bhubaneswar

List-II (Period of development)
(I) Planned as an administrative headquarters after Independence
(II) Developed by the British in the colonial period
(III) Developed in the medieval period as a seat of power
(IV) An ancient town with over 2,000 years of history
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: NCERT groups towns by period: Pataliputra is ancient (IV); Lucknow is medieval (III); Kolkata was developed by the British (II); Bhubaneswar was planned after Independence as an administrative town (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the ancient and medieval towns; (B) swaps Lucknow and Kolkata; (C) swaps Kolkata and Bhubaneswar.
Key point: Other post-Independence planned towns: Chandigarh, Gandhinagar and Dispur (administrative), and Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri and Barauni (industrial).

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Secondary Activities
questions.question: Planned clusters of high-tech industries in landscaped campuses, such as Silicon Valley near San Francisco and Silicon Forest near Seattle, are known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Technopolis
Why: NCERT notes that high-tech industries are often concentrated in planned business parks and that regionally concentrated, self-sustained high-tech clusters are called technopolis; Silicon Valley and Silicon Forest are its examples.
Why not the others: Industrial estates (B) and special economic zones (C) are general policy terms; "agglomeration nodes" (D) is not a term NCERT uses.
Key point: High-tech industry uses intensive research and development and a professional (white collar) workforce.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Primary Activities
questions.question: Commercial livestock rearing on large permanent ranches, organised scientifically and focused on a single type of animal, is mainly practised in:
options: A) The Sahara, the Arabian desert and the Gobi desert of Mongolia
B) The tropical rainforests of the Amazon and Congo basins
C) The Himalayan valleys of India, Nepal and Bhutan
D) New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA
Why: NCERT describes commercial livestock rearing (ranching) as organised and capital intensive, practised on permanent ranches in New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA, rearing sheep, cattle, goats and horses.
Why not the others: (A) are regions of pastoral nomadism; (B) has gathering and shifting cultivation; (C) has transhumance by groups such as Gujjars and Gaddis.
Key point: Ranching is associated with Western cultures; nomadism is a subsistence activity.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Tertiary and Quaternary Activities
questions.question: According to NCERT, which tertiary activity has become the world's single largest in terms of total registered jobs and total revenue?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Tourism
Why: NCERT states that tourism has become the world's single largest tertiary activity in total registered jobs (about 250 million) and total revenue.
Why not the others: Retail (A), finance (C) and telecommunication (D) are major services, but NCERT does not rank them first.
Key point: Tourism supports local services such as accommodation, meals, transport, entertainment and special shops.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Land Resources and Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: Net sown area as a share of reporting area
questions.question: A state has a reporting area of 300 lakh hectares, of which 141 lakh hectares is net sown area. What percentage of the reporting area is net sown?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 47 per cent
Given: reporting area = 300 lakh ha; net sown area = 141 lakh ha.
Step 1: Share = 141 ÷ 300 × 100.
Step 2: = 47 per cent.
Common mistake: giving the share of the land that is not net sown (53 per cent, option A).

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Secondary Activities
questions.question: Industries whose products are used to make other goods — for example iron and steel used to make machinery — are classified by NCERT as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Basic industries
Why: NCERT's classification by product separates basic industries, whose products are used to make other goods, from consumer goods industries, whose products are used directly by consumers.
Why not the others: Consumer goods industries (A) make items such as bread, toothpaste and televisions; footloose (B) and agro-processing (C) are classifications by location and by raw material.
Key point: Iron and steel is a basic industry; a car-making industry that uses steel makes consumer goods.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Population
questions.sub_topic: Categories of workers in the Census
questions.question: For occupational composition, the Census of India divides working population into four categories. Which list is correct?
options: A) Main workers, marginal workers, non-workers and seasonal workers
B) Primary workers, secondary workers, tertiary workers and quaternary workers
C) Cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industry workers and other workers
D) Farm owners, tenants, industrial workers and government employees
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industry workers and other workers
Why: NCERT notes that the working population is divided into four categories — cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers and other workers.
Why not the others: (A) mixes the three-fold division (main, marginal, non-workers) with an invented fourth; (B) is the division of economic sectors, not Census categories; (D) is not a Census grouping.
Key point: A large share of India's workforce is still in the primary sector, with a gradual shift to the secondary and tertiary sectors.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Population
questions.sub_topic: State with the highest density of population
questions.question: In Census 2011, one state recorded about 1,102 persons per square kilometre, the most crowded in India by this measure. Which state was it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bihar
Why: NCERT notes that population density in India ranges from about 1,102 persons per sq km in Bihar to 17 in Arunachal Pradesh.
Why not the others: West Bengal (B) and Kerala (D) are also very dense but below Bihar; Uttar Pradesh (C) is the most populous state, not the densest.
Key point: Most populous ≠ most dense: Uttar Pradesh has the most people, Bihar the most people per sq km.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Human Settlements
questions.question: Isolated huts or hamlets of a few huts in remote jungles, on small hills or on farms and pastures form dispersed settlements. NCERT gives extreme forms of this type in:
options: A) Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala
B) The northern plains of the Ganga and Yamuna
C) The Bundelkhand region and parts of Nagaland
D) The Kerala backwaters and the Gujarat plains only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala
Why: NCERT says extreme forms of dispersed settlements are found in Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala.
Why not the others: The northern plains (B) have clustered settlements; Bundelkhand and Nagaland (C) are NCERT's examples of compact settlements built for defence or water; (D) is not NCERT's description.
Key point: Clustered settlements are compact; dispersed settlements arise from the extremely fragmented nature of terrain and land resources.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Human Development
questions.sub_topic: Access to resources in the HDI
questions.question: In calculating the Human Development Index, a country's performance in "access to resources" is measured in terms of:
options: A) the share of its land under forests and cultivation
B) the number of hospitals and schools per lakh people
C) the value of its minerals and energy reserves per person
D) purchasing power, expressed in US dollars
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) purchasing power, expressed in US dollars
Why: NCERT explains that the HDI uses health (life expectancy at birth), education (access to knowledge) and access to resources, which is measured by purchasing power in US dollars.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the measures used in the HDI.
Key point: The HDI ranges from 0 to 1; the closer to 1, the higher the level of human development.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Planning and Sustainable Development
questions.question: The Drought Prone Area Programme, which aimed to provide employment in drought-prone areas and create productive assets, was started during which Five Year Plan?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Fourth Five Year Plan
Why: NCERT notes that the DPAP was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with these objectives; it was later widened to cover irrigation, land development, afforestation and grassland development.
Why not the others: The First (B), Sixth (C) and Eighth (D) Plans are not linked to the start of DPAP in NCERT.
Key point: Target-area planning also covers Command Area Development and Hill Area Development.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: International Trade
questions.sub_topic: East-coast ports from north to south
questions.question:
Arrange the following ports of India's east coast from north to south:
(A) Paradip
(B) Chennai
(C) Haldia
(D) Visakhapatnam
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: Haldia, downstream of Kolkata on the Hugli, is in West Bengal (C); Paradip is in the Mahanadi delta in Odisha (A); Visakhapatnam is in Andhra Pradesh (D); Chennai is in Tamil Nadu (B).
Why not the others: (B) puts Paradip north of Haldia; (C) puts Visakhapatnam north of Paradip; (D) puts Chennai north of Visakhapatnam.
Key point: Tuticorin (V.O. Chidambaranar) is in the far south of the east coast.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Transport and Communication
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about India's satellite systems:
(A) INSAT, established in 1983, is a multi-purpose system for telecommunication, meteorology and broadcasting.
(B) The IRS satellites are used mainly for monitoring natural resources.
(C) IRS-1A, India's first remote sensing satellite of this series, was launched in 1988.
(D) IRS satellites are used only for television broadcasting and have no role in resource management.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: NCERT describes INSAT (1983) as a multi-purpose system for telecommunication, meteorological observation and data, and broadcasting (A); the IRS system is for resource monitoring (B); IRS-1A was launched in March 1988 (C).
Why not the others: (D) is false — IRS satellites are for resource management, not broadcasting. Options (A) and (C) include it; option (D) leaves out the true statement (B).
Key point: The National Remote Sensing Centre at Hyderabad acquires and processes satellite data.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Mineral and Energy Resources
questions.sub_topic: Location of metallic minerals and coal
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Most of the metallic minerals in India occur in the peninsular plateau region, in the old crystalline rocks.
Reason (R): Over 97 per cent of India's coal reserves occur in the valleys of the Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Both statements are true and are both found in NCERT. But the location of coal reserves does not explain why metallic minerals occur in old crystalline rocks — the two are separate facts.
Why not the others: (A) treats an unrelated fact as the cause; (C) and (D) need one statement to be false.
Key point: Petroleum reserves lie in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Water Resources
questions.sub_topic: Water laws and reuse of water
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) India has about 16 per cent of the world's water resources.
(B) The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1974.
(C) The Environment Protection Act was passed in 1986.
(D) Reclaimed waste-water can be used by industries for cooling and fire fighting.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B) and (C) are the two laws NCERT names, noting that they have not been implemented effectively. (D) NCERT suggests reclaimed waste-water as an attractive option for industrial cooling and fire fighting.
Why not the others: (A) is false — India has about 4 per cent of the world's water resources and about 16 per cent of its population. Options (A) and (B) include it; option (D) leaves out (D).
Key point: Recycling and reuse is one way of improving fresh water availability.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Human Development
questions.question: Which country is the only one in the world to officially proclaim Gross National Happiness as the measure of its progress?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bhutan
Why: NCERT notes that Bhutan is the only country to officially proclaim Gross National Happiness (GNH) as the measure of its progress, alongside material growth.
Why not the others: Nepal (A) and Sri Lanka (B) use conventional measures; Norway (D) is known for a very high HDI, not for GNH.
Key point: GNH stresses the spiritual, non-material and qualitative sides of development.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Population
questions.question: Buddhists are concentrated in Maharashtra, and they are also found in significant numbers in which group of areas, according to NCERT?
options: A) Kerala, Goa and the hill states of Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland
B) Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Tripura and Lahul and Spiti
C) Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, with smaller numbers in Uttarakhand
D) Urban areas of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra, mainly as traders
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Tripura and Lahul and Spiti
Why: NCERT says Buddhists are concentrated in Maharashtra, with other areas of majority in Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Tripura and Lahul and Spiti in Himachal Pradesh.
Why not the others: (A) are areas with large Christian populations; (C) is where Sikhs are concentrated; (D) is where Jains are concentrated.
Key point: Hindus are the majority in most states; the distribution of minorities is concentrated in particular regions.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Slums in Indian cities are found mainly in well-planned central areas with good housing and civic amenities.
Reason (R): Many rural–urban migrants who cannot afford proper housing settle in slums.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: The Reason is true — NCERT describes slums as the home of poor migrants forced to live in environmentally incompatible and degraded areas. The Assertion is false — slums have the least-developed residential areas, with dilapidated houses, poor sanitation and few civic amenities, often in unplanned areas.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) need a true Assertion; (C) needs a false Reason.
Key point: Dharavi in Mumbai is NCERT's case study of a slum.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: International Trade
questions.question: The practice of selling a commodity in another country at a price that differs from its price at home, and is not related to its cost of production, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Dumping
Why: NCERT defines dumping as selling a commodity in two countries at prices that differ, for reasons not related to costs. It can harm producers in the importing country.
Why not the others: Protectionism (A) is the use of barriers against imports; bilateral trade (B) is trade between two countries; free trade (D) is the removal of trade barriers.
Key point: Countries need to be watchful about dumped goods once trade is opened up.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
questions.question: As people understand their environment better and develop more efficient technology, they move from a state of necessity to a state of freedom, create possibilities with the resources around them and build a cultural landscape. This view of the human–nature relationship is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Possibilism
Why: NCERT calls this possibilism — nature provides opportunities, and humans use them to create possibilities, leaving imprints such as farms, towns and roads.
Why not the others: Determinism (A) sees nature as controlling humans; neo-determinism (C) is Griffith Taylor's middle path; "naturalisation of humans" (D) describes the early stage when people adapted to nature with simple technology.
Key point: Possibilism = humanisation of nature; determinism = naturalisation of humans.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Tertiary and Quaternary Activities
questions.question: Patients from other countries come to India for treatment such as heart surgery and joint replacement because good care is available at much lower cost. This trend is described in NCERT as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Medical tourism
Why: NCERT describes medical tourism — overseas patients travelling to Indian cities for treatment in leading hospitals — as an important tertiary activity.
Why not the others: KPO (A) and BPO (B) move work, not patients; telemedicine (D) gives medical advice from a distance without the patient travelling.
Key point: India is a leading country of medical tourism; such travel also brings revenue to the host country.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
questions.sub_topic: Approaches to human geography over time
questions.question:
Arrange the following approaches in human geography in the order in which they became prominent, from the earliest to the latest:
(A) Spatial organisation, marked by the use of computers and statistical tools
(B) Areal differentiation, identifying how one region differs from another
(C) Emergence of the humanistic, radical and behavioural schools
(D) Regional analysis, describing regions in all their aspects
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (A), (C)
Why: NCERT's table gives regional analysis in the later colonial period (D), areal differentiation in the inter-war period of the 1930s (B), spatial organisation in the late 1950s–1960s, the quantitative revolution (A), and the humanistic, radical and behavioural schools in the 1970s (C).
Why not the others: (B) puts areal differentiation before regional analysis; (C) puts the quantitative phase before the inter-war phase; (D) puts the 1970s schools before the 1960s.
Key point: Exploration and description came first (early colonial period) and post-modernism came last (1990s).

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Land Resources and Agriculture
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Crop)
(A) Tea
(B) Coffee
(C) Jute
(D) Sugarcane

List-II (Leading state in NCERT)
(I) West Bengal
(II) Uttar Pradesh
(III) Assam
(IV) Karnataka
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: NCERT: Assam has more than half the area under tea (III); Karnataka produces more than two-thirds of India's coffee (IV); West Bengal produces most of the jute (I); Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifths of the sugarcane (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps tea and coffee; (C) swaps jute and sugarcane; (D) swaps coffee and jute.
Key point: Tea and coffee are plantation crops; jute and cotton are fibre crops.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Primary Activities
questions.question: In some market-gardening regions, farmers specialise in vegetables only, and the distance of their farms from the market is decided by the distance a truck can cover overnight. Such farming is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Truck farming
Why: NCERT calls this truck farming — vegetable farming located within an overnight truck journey of urban markets.
Why not the others: Mixed farming (A) combines crops and livestock; factory farming (C) is stall-fed rearing of livestock, especially poultry and cattle; dairy farming (D) rears milch animals.
Key point: Market gardening and horticulture are practised in densely populated industrial districts with high-income markets.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Transport and Communication
questions.question: The Trans-Canadian Highway links:
options: A) Vancouver in British Columbia with St. John's in Newfoundland
B) Edmonton in Canada with Anchorage in Alaska
C) Halifax on the Atlantic with Vancouver on the Pacific coast
D) Montreal in Quebec with Winnipeg in the Prairie provinces
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Vancouver in British Columbia with St. John's in Newfoundland
Why: NCERT states that the Trans-Canadian Highway links Vancouver in British Columbia (west coast) with St. John's in Newfoundland (east coast).
Why not the others: Edmonton–Anchorage (B) is the Alaskan Highway; Halifax–Vancouver (C) is the route of the Trans-Canadian railway; (D) is only part of the country.
Key point: The Pan-American Highway will connect South America, Central America and the USA–Canada.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Human Development
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Human Poverty Index, which is related to the HDI?
options: A) It measures the shortfall in human development and is a non-income measure
B) It counts only the people whose income is below a fixed money poverty line
C) It ranks countries by gross national product per person in US dollars
D) It measures happiness and the cultural and spiritual well-being of people
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It measures the shortfall in human development and is a non-income measure
Why: NCERT says the Human Poverty Index measures the shortfall in human development. It is a non-income measure, using the chance of not surviving to age 40, the adult illiteracy rate, the lack of access to clean water and the number of underweight small children.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are income measures; (D) describes Gross National Happiness.
Key point: The HDI measures attainment; the Human Poverty Index measures shortfall.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Mineral and Energy Resources
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Oilfield)
(A) Digboi
(B) Ankaleshwar
(C) Mumbai High
(D) Krishna–Godavari basin

List-II (Location)
(I) Offshore, in the Arabian Sea
(II) Assam
(III) The east coast
(IV) Gujarat
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Digboi (with Naharkatiya and Moran) is in Assam (II); Ankaleshwar (with Kalol and Mehsana) is in Gujarat (IV); Mumbai High is offshore, about 160 km from Mumbai (I); the Krishna–Godavari and Kaveri basins on the east coast are newer finds (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Digboi and Ankaleshwar; (B) swaps Mumbai High and the east-coast basin; (D) swaps Ankaleshwar and Mumbai High.
Key point: Mumbai High was discovered in 1973 and production began in 1976.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Land Resources and Agriculture
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the problems of Indian agriculture:
(A) Farming in unirrigated areas depends heavily on the erratic monsoon.
(B) Crop yields in India are low compared with international levels.
(C) Farm holdings are becoming larger with each generation because land is being consolidated everywhere.
(D) Many farmers produce mainly for their own consumption, so agriculture lacks commercialisation.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: NCERT lists dependence on the erratic monsoon (A), low productivity (B) and lack of commercialisation (D) among the problems of Indian agriculture.
Why not the others: (C) is false — farm holdings are small and are getting more fragmented as land is divided among heirs. Options (A), (B) and (C) include it.
Key point: Other problems — constraints of finance and indebtedness, lack of land reforms, underemployment and degradation of cultivable land.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Primary Activities
questions.sub_topic: Animals of pastoral nomads by region
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Region)
(A) Tibet
(B) The Andes
(C) The Arctic and sub-Arctic
(D) The Sahara

List-II (Main animal of pastoral nomads)
(I) Reindeer
(II) Camel
(III) Llama
(IV) Yak
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: NCERT notes that yaks (Tibet) and llamas (Andes) are reared in mountain areas, reindeer in the Arctic and sub-Arctic, and sheep, goats and camels in the Sahara and Asian deserts.
Why not the others: (A) swaps the Andes and the Arctic; (B) swaps Tibet and the Andes; (C) swaps the Arctic and the Sahara.
Key point: The choice of animal depends on the geographical conditions of the region.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Transport and Communication
questions.question: Pawan Hans, which provides helicopter services to the petroleum sector, is widely used for tourism and in hilly areas, especially in:
options: A) The western desert of Rajasthan
B) The coastal plains of Gujarat
C) The Deccan plateau of Maharashtra
D) The north-eastern region of India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The north-eastern region of India
Why: NCERT notes that Pawan Hans is the helicopter service operating in hilly areas and is widely used by tourists in the north-eastern sector; it also serves the petroleum sector.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the regions NCERT names for Pawan Hans.
Key point: Air transport in India is managed by the Airports Authority of India.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Water Resources
questions.question: Which sector accounts for by far the largest share of the use of surface water in India?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Agriculture
Why: NCERT notes that agriculture accounts for most of the surface water and groundwater used in India — about 89 per cent of surface water use.
Why not the others: Industry (A), domestic use (C) and power (D) use much smaller shares, though their demand is rising.
Key point: Rising demand from industry and households will increase competition for water.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: International Trade
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Type of port)
(A) Port of call
(B) Packet station
(C) Out port
(D) Oil port

List-II (Example)
(I) Piraeus, serving Athens
(II) Maracaibo in Venezuela
(III) Honolulu in the Pacific
(IV) Dover in England
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: NCERT's examples: ports of call such as Aden and Honolulu are stopping points on main sea routes (III); packet stations such as Dover and Calais carry passengers and mail across short distances (IV); out ports such as Piraeus serve a city that lies inland — Athens (I); oil ports include Maracaibo in Venezuela (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the port of call and the packet station; (C) swaps the packet station and the out port; (D) swaps the out port and the oil port.
Key point: Ports are also classified by cargo handled (industrial, commercial, comprehensive) and by location (inland, out ports).

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Primary Activities
questions.sub_topic: Collective farming in the former USSR
questions.question: The collective farming model introduced in the former Soviet Union, in which farmers pooled land, livestock and labour and shared the produce, was called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Kolkhoz
Why: NCERT notes that collective farming, called Kolkhoz, was introduced in the former Soviet Union to improve on the inefficiency of earlier farming methods and to boost production.
Why not the others: The ejido (A) and kibbutz (B) are collective systems of Mexico and Israel not described in NCERT; ladang (D) is shifting cultivation in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Key point: In collective farming, the government fixes the targets and buys the produce at fixed prices.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Secondary Activities
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the classification of manufacturing by size:
(A) Cottage manufacturing is the smallest unit, in which artisans use local raw materials and simple tools at home.
(B) Small-scale manufacturing uses local raw materials, simple power-driven machines and semi-skilled labour.
(C) Large-scale manufacturing involves large markets, varied raw materials, huge energy use and assembly-line mass production.
(D) Large-scale manufacturing first developed in the river valleys of Asia, long before the Industrial Revolution.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) follow NCERT's description of household (cottage), small-scale and large-scale manufacturing.
Why not the others: (D) is false — NCERT says large-scale manufacturing developed in the last 200 years, in the United Kingdom, north-eastern USA and Europe. Options (A) and (D) include it; option (C) leaves out the true statement (A).
Key point: Small-scale manufacturing provides employment and raises local purchasing power; India, China and Indonesia support it.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: Transport and Communication
questions.question: The ocean route that links north-eastern USA with north-western Europe, carries about one-fourth of the world's foreign trade and is the busiest in the world, is known as the "Big Trunk Route". It is the:
options: B) Cape of Good Hope Route
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Northern Atlantic Route
Why: NCERT describes the Northern Atlantic Sea Route as the busiest in the world, linking the two industrially developed regions of north-eastern USA and north-western Europe; it is called the Big Trunk Route.
Why not the others: The Mediterranean–Indian Ocean route (A) passes through the Suez Canal; the Cape of Good Hope route (B) goes round southern Africa; the North Pacific route (C) links North America with Asia.
Key point: Both coasts of the North Atlantic have highly developed ports and harbours.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Land Resources and Agriculture
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In its early years, the Green Revolution was largely confined to irrigated areas such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
Reason (R): The high-yielding varieties of seeds needed assured irrigation along with chemical fertilisers and pesticides.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Both are true. NCERT notes that the new technology of HYV seeds, fertilisers and pesticides was first applied in irrigated areas, because the seeds gave high yields only with assured water — which explains the Assertion.
Why not the others: (B) would need the Reason to be unrelated; (C) and (D) need one statement to be false.
Key point: The Green Revolution raised food grain output but widened regional inequality and later caused land degradation.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Transport and Communication
questions.question:
Arrange the following railway gauges of India from the widest to the narrowest:
(A) Metre gauge
(B) Narrow gauge of 0.610 metre
(C) Broad gauge
(D) Narrow gauge of 0.762 metre
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: NCERT gives broad gauge as 1.676 m (C), metre gauge as 1.000 m (A), and narrow gauge as 0.762 m (D) and 0.610 m (B).
Why not the others: (A) puts the 0.762 m narrow gauge above the metre gauge; (B) starts with metre gauge; (D) reverses the two narrow gauges.
Key point: Under Project Unigauge, metre and narrow gauges are being converted to broad gauge.

questions.topic: India: People and Economy: Mineral and Energy Resources
questions.question: High-quality mica is obtained from the lower Hazaribagh plateau. This area lies in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Jharkhand
Why: NCERT notes that mica is found in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan, and that high-quality mica comes from the lower Hazaribagh plateau in Jharkhand.
Why not the others: Andhra Pradesh (A), with Nellore, and Rajasthan (C) also produce mica, but the Hazaribagh plateau is in Jharkhand; Odisha (D) is not a main mica state.
Key point: Mica is used in the electrical and electronic industries because it is a good insulator.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: The World Population
questions.sub_topic: Year of the highest natural growth rate
questions.question:
Study the following table and answer the question that follows.

Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) of Country X, 1900–2020 (per thousand population; there is no migration; figures are illustrative)

| Year | CBR | CDR |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | 40 | 37 |
| 1930 | 39 | 30 |
| 1960 | 36 | 15 |
| 1990 | 22 | 9 |
| 2020 | 12 | 10 |

Question: In which year was the natural growth rate of Country X the highest?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1960
Given: natural growth = CBR − CDR.
Step 1: 1900: 3; 1930: 9; 1960: 21; 1990: 13; 2020: 2 (per thousand).
Step 2: The highest is 21 per thousand, in 1960.
Common mistake: picking 1930 (option A) because its birth rate is close to the highest; growth depends on the gap between births and deaths.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: The World Population
questions.sub_topic: Features of the first stage of demographic transition
questions.question:
Study the following table and answer the question that follows.

Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) of Country X, 1900–2020 (per thousand population; there is no migration; figures are illustrative)

| Year | CBR | CDR |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | 40 | 37 |
| 1930 | 39 | 30 |
| 1960 | 36 | 15 |
| 1990 | 22 | 9 |
| 2020 | 12 | 10 |

Question: The figures for 1900 show Country X in the first stage of demographic transition. Which description fits that stage, according to NCERT?
options: A) High fertility and high mortality; people are mostly farmers, and life expectancy is low
B) High fertility but falling mortality, because sanitation and health care are improving
C) Low fertility and low mortality; the population is mostly urban and literate
D) Falling fertility and rising mortality, so the population shrinks every decade
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) High fertility and high mortality; people are mostly farmers, and life expectancy is low
Why: In the first stage, high fertility is balanced by high mortality, so the population grows slowly; most people are engaged in agriculture, large families are an asset, life expectancy is low and technology is simple.
Why not the others: (B) is the second stage; (C) is the last stage; (D) is not a stage of the model.
Key point: In 1900, Country X's CBR (40) and CDR (37) are both high, giving slow growth.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: The World Population
questions.sub_topic: Cause of rapid growth between 1930 and 1960
questions.question:
Study the following table and answer the question that follows.

Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) of Country X, 1900–2020 (per thousand population; there is no migration; figures are illustrative)

| Year | CBR | CDR |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | 40 | 37 |
| 1930 | 39 | 30 |
| 1960 | 36 | 15 |
| 1990 | 22 | 9 |
| 2020 | 12 | 10 |

Question: Between 1930 and 1960 the gap between Country X's birth and death rates widened sharply. In terms of demographic transition, the most likely reason is that:
options: A) people deliberately began to limit family size as they moved to cities
B) the birth rate rose steeply because of a large wave of immigration
C) both fertility and mortality fell together at about the same pace
D) sanitation and health improved, cutting deaths while births stayed high
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) sanitation and health improved, cutting deaths while births stayed high
Why: The CDR fell from 30 to 15 while the CBR stayed high (39 to 36). NCERT describes this as the second stage: improvements in sanitation and health conditions reduce mortality while fertility remains high at first, so the population grows rapidly.
Why not the others: Deliberate control of family size (A) belongs to the last stage; the table assumes no migration (B); births and deaths did not fall at the same pace (C).
Key point: The widening gap between births and deaths is what drives the population explosion of stage two.

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: The World Population
questions.question:
Study the following table and answer the question that follows.

Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) of Country X, 1900–2020 (per thousand population; there is no migration; figures are illustrative)

| Year | CBR | CDR |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | 40 | 37 |
| 1930 | 39 | 30 |
| 1960 | 36 | 15 |
| 1990 | 22 | 9 |
| 2020 | 12 | 10 |

Question: What was the annual natural growth rate of Country X in 1990, expressed as a percentage?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.3 per cent
Given: in 1990, CBR = 22 and CDR = 9 per thousand.
Step 1: Natural growth = 22 − 9 = 13 per thousand.
Step 2: As a percentage, 13 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 1.3 per cent.
Common mistake: reading 13 per thousand as 13 per cent (option C), or adding the two rates (31 per thousand = 3.1 per cent, option A).

questions.topic: Fundamentals of Human Geography: The World Population
questions.sub_topic: Features of the last stage of demographic transition
questions.question:
Study the following table and answer the question that follows.

Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) of Country X, 1900–2020 (per thousand population; there is no migration; figures are illustrative)

| Year | CBR | CDR |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | 40 | 37 |
| 1930 | 39 | 30 |
| 1960 | 36 | 15 |
| 1990 | 22 | 9 |
| 2020 | 12 | 10 |

Question: By 2020 Country X had reached the last stage of demographic transition. Which of the following is NOT a feature of that stage, according to NCERT?
options: A) Both fertility and mortality have declined to low levels
B) The population is stable or grows only slowly
C) Most people work on farms and value large families as an asset
D) People are largely urban, literate and deliberately limit family size
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Most people work on farms and value large families as an asset
Why: Option (C) describes the first stage, not the last. NCERT says that in the last stage both fertility and mortality decline considerably, the population is either stable or grows slowly, and it becomes urbanised, literate and technically skilled, deliberately controlling family size.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are all features of the last stage.
Key point: In 2020, Country X's CBR (12) and CDR (10) are both low — natural growth is only 2 per thousand.
